unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 5! This unit takes you into the great outdoors. You will explore topics connected to outdoor adventures, nature and environmental protection. Whether it is hiking through a forest, camping beside a river, or working together to protect the natural world, this unit gives you the language skills to describe, discuss and write about these experiences with confidence.
unit.learningPath: Begin with the Vocabulary companion and learn the twenty-nine unit words a few at a time, saying each example aloud. Work through the six grammar lessons: -ing forms, the present and past passive, modal verbs with the passive, future forms, and comparatives and superlatives. Read "Guardians of the Green", the eco-club field reports and the three-part story "The Weight of a Choice", answering the comprehension questions with evidence from the text. Complete the writing workshop, the speaking and listening tasks and the activities, then finish with the quiz and the Check Your Learning self-assessment.

readings.title: Guardians of the Green
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
On a cool Saturday morning in March, Amal and her Year 7 classmates gathered at the school gate. They were about to begin a two-day expedition to the Boni National Reserve, one of Kenya's least-visited protected forests. Teacher Yasmin had been planning the trip for months.
"Today," she announced, adjusting her backpack, "we are not just visitors. We are guardians. Everything we see, we must protect."
The journey took three hours by bus. When the students finally stepped onto the forest trail, the air felt different — cooler, damper, and full of unfamiliar sounds. Tall trees stretched upward, their branches forming a thick canopy that blocked most of the sunlight. Birds called from hidden perches, and somewhere in the distance, a stream gurgled over rocks.
Amal, one of the keenest hikers, was the first to notice the damage. Along the edge of the trail, several large trees had been cut down. Their stumps were pale and raw, surrounded by scattered branches. "Deforestation," she whispered to her friend Nora. "Someone has been logging here illegally."
Teacher Yasmin gathered the group. "This is exactly what I wanted you to see," she said seriously. "The Boni Forest is home to rare animals and hundreds of plant species. When trees are removed, the entire ecosystem suffers. Birds lose their nests. The soil washes away in the rain. Rivers become polluted with mud. Biodiversity decreases."
She asked the students to take notes and photographs to document what they observed. They would use this evidence later to create environmental awareness materials for their school and community.
That afternoon, a local ranger named Tariq joined the group. He explained how conservation efforts were helping the forest recover. "We have established a tree-planting programme," he said. "Every month, volunteers plant two hundred seedlings. Protecting the forest is not one person's job — it requires collaboration."
The students set up their campsite near a clearing. They collected firewood that had already fallen — they did not break any living branches. They filtered water from the stream and cooked a simple meal of rice, beans and chapati. As the sun set, the sky turned from gold to deep violet, and the first stars appeared. Leo pointed upward. "Look at that," he said quietly. "You cannot see stars like this in the city."
Around the campfire, Teacher Yasmin asked each student to share one thing they had learned. "I learned that protecting nature is not just about big organisations," said Amal. "It starts with us — with small choices, like not littering, like planting a tree, like speaking up when something is wrong."
The next morning, the group joined the ranger's team to plant thirty saplings along the damaged section of the trail. Each student dug a hole, placed a seedling carefully inside, and covered the roots with soil. It was hard, rewarding work.
On the bus home, the students were tired but changed. They had seen the beauty of the natural world and the threats it faces. They understood that sustainability is not just a word in a textbook — it is a responsibility. And they were ready to become the guardians their teacher had asked them to be.

readings.title: Eco-Club Field Reports
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Read the two field reports below closely. Both were written for the school newsletter after recent eco-club trips, and both use the future forms and comparative language you are learning in this unit.
Report 1: Counting birds along the river, by Daniel
Last weekend, our school's eco-club went on a nature walk along the Jubba River. We left at seven in the morning and walked for about four kilometres. Along the way, we identified fifteen different species of birds and collected three bags of litter from the riverbank. Our guide explained that the river's water level has been dropping because trees along the bank have been cut down. Without tree roots, the soil erodes and the river becomes shallower. We are going to return next month to plant fifty mangrove seedlings along the riverbank.
Report 2: Choosing our next campsite, by Maya
The eco-club must choose between two campsites for the end-of-term trip, and the committee has asked members to compare them before Friday's vote. Campsite A is next to a quiet lake. It has shade from tall acacia trees and a clean water supply. However, it is far from the main road, so it takes longer to reach. Campsite B is near the road and easy to access. It has modern toilet facilities but very little shade, and the area can be noisy because of passing vehicles. The winning campsite will be booked before the holidays begin.
When you compare the campsites, build sentences like these: "Campsite A is quieter than Campsite B." "Campsite B is easier to reach than Campsite A." Then decide which campsite you would prefer, and explain your choice using because.

readings.title: The Weight of a Choice, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The air at Kasisira Secondary School was dry and warm on the morning the student prefect elections were announced. Posters flapped on walls, dust blew over the netball court, and excited whispers filled the corridor. Among the crowd was sixteen-year-old Jamal, tall and calm, with a sharp mind and quiet confidence.
Jamal had never planned to lead. But when his classmates began asking him to run for Head Prefect, he could not help but consider it.
"People respect you," said Imani, his friend. "You listen. You don't show off. You're fair."
At first, Jamal hesitated. Leadership meant responsibility. And mistakes.
That night, he lay awake evaluating the consequences. Becoming Head Prefect would mean sacrificing some free time, facing criticism, and being held to a higher standard. But it would also be a chance to help fix real problems — like the broken water tank or the crumbling library roof.
The next morning, he signed the nomination form. His campaign slogan was simple: Integrity is action.
His main opponent was Nadir, a clever boy who was known for charm and style. Nadir's speeches were full of energy. But some students whispered that Nadir had once been caught trying to plagiarize an essay from the internet.
"I hope he's changed," Jamal said.
The week before voting, candidates had to give a speech. Jamal stood on the assembly platform and spoke clearly.
"We have problems," he said. "Water is scarce. Classrooms are crowded. Our voices must be heard. I will not promise perfection, but I will promise effort. I will listen, act, and always acknowledge when I am wrong."
The students clapped — not loudly, but sincerely.
Two days later, the results were announced: Jamal had won. The head teacher handed him a badge, and the whole school cheered.
His leadership began well. He organised a clean-up day. He met with teachers about better exam preparation. He even worked to establish a suggestion box system.
But a month later, trouble came.
During break, Imani ran to him, breathless. "Jamal — someone has stolen the lab projector."
The projector, donated by a local NGO, was one of the school's few digital tools. Without it, the science department would suffer.
The news spread fast. The head teacher was furious. "This is a significant loss," she said. "The police have been informed."
Later that day, Jamal sat in the staffroom, thinking. How could something so valuable be stolen without notice?
One teacher suggested, "Security needs to be stricter. Clearly, rules are being infringed."
Investigating the theft became Jamal's top priority. He interviewed students, examined the storage room, and reviewed the gate logs. The cameras did not work — that system had never been repaired.
By Friday, suspicion turned toward a group of Form 4 boys who were often late and had once been found skipping lessons behind the kitchen. Among them was a boy named Zane, a known trickster.
Zane was called in. He denied everything.
But that night, Jamal received an anonymous note under his dorm pillow:
"The projector was hidden. Behind the old library."
He raced there with two friends. Behind the crumbling shelves, wrapped in a sack, was the missing device. Still working. Not stolen — just moved.
But why?

readings.passageScript:
A week later, a Form 3 boy came forward and confessed: "We borrowed it. To practise PowerPoint. For a regional ICT competition."
Jamal was shocked. "Why not ask?"
The boy shrugged. "No one listens. We thought we'd be admonished. So we hid it."
Jamal knew the school would want to punish them. But he also knew their intention was not to harm.
He wrote a report to the head teacher. In it, he did not try to embellish the facts. He explained everything honestly and suggested a solution: "The boys should apologise publicly, and they must fix what they've broken — but their motive must be considered."
The head teacher nodded slowly. "This is a reasonable proposal. Well evaluated."
The boys were not expelled. Instead, they helped repair the lab room and wrote a guide for using the projector.
Later, Jamal told Imani, "Sometimes, to lead is to alleviate conflict, not increase it."
But the story did not end there.
Two weeks before the school's Independence Day event, Jamal faced another challenge. The student drama group wanted to perform a play that had been written by a famous Ugandan playwright. But one teacher raised a concern: "We must request permission. This play is copyrighted. Using it without permission is plagiarizing."
Some students were angry. "Who will know?" one asked. "Let's just imitate it."
Jamal shook his head. "We must not pretend. Copying must be avoided. Integrity is not just for show."
Instead, he suggested the students write their own play — about school life. He offered to help them collaborate.
Writing it was not easy. Ideas clashed. Tempers rose. Some students nearly quit. But eventually, a script was developed: funny, honest, and original.
During the performance, laughter echoed in the hall. Teachers smiled. Parents clapped. And when the principal stood to speak, she said, "This is one of the most significant student efforts I have seen."
A local education officer, who had attended, requested a copy to share with other schools.
After the event, Jamal reflected. Leading a school was like trying to sustain a flame in the wind. Not flashy, but steady.
Still, challenges continued. During exam week, two students were caught trying to sneak answer sheets.
"They must be suspended," said one teacher. "Cheating must be punished."
But Jamal asked, "What led to this?"
After speaking with the students, he learned both were under pressure. One cared for three siblings. The other worked nights to help at his uncle's shop.
"It doesn't excuse them," Jamal said, "but understanding the cause can help us respond better."
He recommended that, alongside punishment, the boys be offered support. A reading club was started. Evening prep hours were extended. Discipline was balanced with help.
Certainly, not everyone agreed. Some called Jamal naive.
But others began to follow his example.
One teacher said, "Jamal reminds us that solving a problem is harder than punishing it — but far more valuable."

readings.title: The Weight of a Choice, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Another challenge came when the school's debate club invited students to argue whether leaders should be allowed to relinquish power before their term ends.
Jamal, listening from the back, wondered: should he step down now, in his final term, to let others grow?
He wrote in his diary: "Is knowing when to lead as important as knowing when to leave?"
The next week, he gathered the prefects.
"I believe it's time," he said. "I will abdicate my role early so that a new leader can take over — with fresh ideas."
Imani gasped. "Why?"
Jamal smiled. "Because true leadership is about growth — not power."
His decision was not forced. It was respected.
His replacement was a younger student, attentive and eager.
At the final assembly, the principal spoke.
"Jamal has demonstrated the kind of leadership that teaches others to lead. His actions will not be forgotten. He leaves behind not just policies — but a culture."
The hall stood to applaud.
As Jamal walked off stage, badge in hand, he felt no regret. Only peace.
His time had ended, but the values he planted would remain — like seeds, waiting for the next rain.

comprehension.question: Where did Amal's class go on their expedition, and how long did the bus journey take?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They went to the Boni National Reserve, one of Kenya's least-visited protected forests, and the bus journey took three hours.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question: the destination appears in the opening paragraph and the journey time at the start of the third paragraph.

comprehension.question: What damage did Amal notice along the edge of the trail?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She noticed that several large trees had been cut down illegally, leaving pale, raw stumps surrounded by scattered branches.
comprehension.explanation: The learner must locate the description of the logging damage and recognise that Amal names it deforestation.

comprehension.question: According to Teacher Yasmin, what happens to the ecosystem when trees are removed? Give at least three effects.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Birds lose their nests, the soil washes away in the rain, rivers become polluted with mud, and biodiversity decreases.
comprehension.explanation: The four effects are listed in Teacher Yasmin's speech beside the tree stumps; any three of them earn the mark.

comprehension.question: How did the students take care of the environment at their campsite?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They collected only firewood that had already fallen, did not break any living branches, and filtered water from the stream.
comprehension.explanation: This checks the campsite paragraph, where the students' careful, low-impact choices are described one by one.

comprehension.question: In Daniel's river report, why has the river's water level been dropping?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Trees along the bank have been cut down, and without tree roots the soil erodes and the river becomes shallower.
comprehension.explanation: The guide's explanation links tree loss to erosion; the learner must connect both steps of the cause-and-effect chain.

comprehension.question: What is the eco-club going to do next month, and which future form does Daniel use to say so?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They are going to return to plant fifty mangrove seedlings along the riverbank; Daniel uses going to because it is a plan the club has already decided.
comprehension.explanation: This pairs retrieval with grammar awareness: the final sentence of Report 1 uses the going to form for a settled plan.

comprehension.question: Why did Jamal's classmates want him to run for Head Prefect? Name two qualities they saw in him.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Imani said that people respected him because he listened, did not show off, and was fair.
comprehension.explanation: The qualities are listed in Imani's direct speech near the beginning of the story; any two of them are enough.

comprehension.question: What did the anonymous note under Jamal's pillow say, and what did he discover because of it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The note said the projector was hidden behind the old library, and there Jamal found the missing device wrapped in a sack, still working.
comprehension.explanation: The learner must join the note's message to the discovery scene that closes part 1: the projector was moved, not stolen.

comprehension.question: How did Jamal's report about the projector show balanced judgement? Support your answer with evidence.
comprehension.correctAnswer: He refused to embellish the facts and explained everything honestly, yet he also asked for the boys' motive to be considered alongside the public apology and repairs.
comprehension.explanation: A strong answer weighs both sides of the report: honesty about the wrongdoing and fairness about the intention behind it.

comprehension.question: Why did the drama group end up writing their own play instead of performing the famous playwright's work?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Performing the copyrighted play without permission would have been plagiarizing, so Jamal persuaded the group to collaborate on an original play about school life.
comprehension.explanation: The learner must connect the teacher's copyright warning with Jamal's insistence that copying must be avoided.

comprehension.question: Why did Jamal decide to abdicate his role as Head Prefect before his term ended?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He believed that true leadership is about growth rather than power, so he stepped down early to let a new leader take over with fresh ideas.
comprehension.explanation: The debate about relinquishing power prompts Jamal's diary question, and his announcement to the prefects gives the reason directly.

comprehension.question: Explain the meaning of the story's closing image: the values Jamal planted would remain like seeds, waiting for the next rain.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Although Jamal's term was over, the honesty and fairness he modelled would keep growing in the school, just as planted seeds grow when the rain finally comes.
comprehension.explanation: This evaluative question asks the learner to unpack the seed metaphor: values, like seeds, outlast the person who planted them.

grammar.title: -ing Forms (Gerunds and Participles)
grammar.explanation: The -ing form of a verb can act as a noun, called a gerund. In this unit you use gerunds in three places: as the subject of a sentence, as the object after certain verbs, and after prepositions — all of which are common when writing about outdoor activities.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
How to form the -ing form: most verbs add -ing directly (walk → walking, read → reading); verbs ending in silent -e drop the e (hike → hiking, explore → exploring); short consonant-vowel-consonant verbs double the final consonant (run → running, swim → swimming, plan → planning); verbs ending in -ie change -ie to -y (die → dying, lie → lying).
Use 1 — as the subject of a sentence: "Hiking is a great way to explore nature." "Recycling helps reduce waste in our communities." "Protecting endangered animals requires effort from everyone."
Use 2 — as the object after verbs such as enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, recommend, keep, practise, consider, mind, imagine, risk, miss and deny: "I enjoy exploring new places." "We should avoid wasting water." "She finished writing her report on deforestation." "Can you imagine living without clean water?"
Use 3 — after prepositions such as in, on, at, by, about, without, before, after, for, of and instead of: "She is interested in learning about wildlife." "They succeeded by working as a team." "Before leaving, we checked for litter." "Instead of complaining, he offered a solution."
grammar.commonMistake: Using the infinitive where the -ing form is needed: "She is interested in to learn" and "I enjoy to read" are wrong — after a preposition, and after verbs such as enjoy, the verb must be "learning" and "reading".
grammar.memoryTip: A gerund is an action noun: if you can swap the -ing word for "it", as in "Camping is fun" becoming "It is fun", the -ing word is working as a noun.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with the -ing form of the verb in brackets: 1) ______ (plant) trees helps clean the air. 2) I enjoy ______ (camp) in the mountains. 3) She is afraid of ______ (climb) steep hills. 4) ______ (protect) the environment is everyone's duty. 5) They avoided ______ (pollute) the river. 6) After ______ (walk) for two hours, we rested. 7) He suggested ______ (use) solar panels at school. 8) ______ (reduce) waste starts with small daily choices.
Part B — more gap-fills from your lesson booklet: 9) We enjoy ______ (observe) birds in their natural habitat. 10) After ______ (hike) for three hours, we reached the summit. 11) He avoids ______ (waste) water whenever possible. 12) They are thinking about ______ (start) a recycling programme at school.
Part C — write three sentences of your own: one -ing form as a subject, one as an object after a verb, and one after a preposition.

Answer Key (for self-checking):
Part A: 1) Planting 2) camping 3) climbing 4) Protecting 5) polluting 6) walking 7) using 8) Reducing.
Part B: 9) observing 10) hiking 11) wasting 12) starting.
Part C: This part is open-ended — you write three sentences of your own. Self-check using the memory tip: for the subject example, can you swap the -ing word for "it" (e.g., "Camping is fun" becomes "It is fun")? For the object example, does your -ing word directly follow a verb such as enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, consider or similar? For the preposition example, does your -ing word directly follow a preposition such as in, on, at, by, about, without, before, after, for, of or instead of, rather than a to-infinitive?

grammar.title: Present Passive
grammar.explanation: The present passive puts the focus on the action or the thing that receives it, rather than on who does it. It suits scientific and environmental writing, where the process matters more than the person.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: subject + is/am/are + past participle, with an optional by-phrase for the agent.
"The forest is protected by law." "Trees are planted every spring." "Plastic is recycled at this facility." "The water is tested for pollution regularly."
The agent can be left out when it is unknown or unimportant: "The water is tested regularly."
Active versus passive: "Rangers protect the forest." becomes "The forest is protected by rangers."; "Volunteers plant trees every year." becomes "Trees are planted every year."; "Factories pollute the river." becomes "The river is polluted by factories."
grammar.commonMistake: Choosing the wrong form of "to be" or dropping the past participle: "The trees is planted" needs are because trees is plural, and "The car is drive" needs the participle driven.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask "Who does it?" — if the answer is unknown or unimportant, turn the sentence round: the receiver moves to the front and the verb becomes is or are plus the past participle.
grammar.practice:
Part A — rewrite each active sentence in the present passive: 1) Scientists study endangered species. 2) The school recycles paper and plastic. 3) People use solar energy to power homes. 4) Rangers monitor the wildlife in the park. 5) Farmers grow organic vegetables without chemicals.
Part B — write two present passive sentences of your own about how waste is handled in your community.

Answer Key (for self-checking):
Part A: 1) Endangered species are studied by scientists. 2) Paper and plastic are recycled by the school. 3) Solar energy is used to power homes. 4) The wildlife in the park is monitored by rangers. 5) Organic vegetables are grown without chemicals.
Part B: This part is open-ended — you write two present passive sentences of your own about how waste is handled in your community. Self-check: does each sentence follow subject + is/am/are + past participle (for example, "Waste is collected every Tuesday" or "Plastic bottles are recycled at the local centre"), including a by-phrase only if the agent actually matters?

grammar.title: Past Passive
grammar.explanation: The past passive reports what was done to someone or something in the past. It is very useful for reporting events, describing history, and writing about environmental changes that have already happened.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: subject + was/were + past participle, with an optional by-phrase.
"The national park was established in 1985." "Two hundred trees were planted by volunteers last month." "The river was polluted by factory waste." "The damaged trail was repaired before the rainy season."
Use was for singular subjects (he, she, it, the park) and were for plural subjects (they, we, the trees).
Active versus passive: "The storm destroyed the bridge." becomes "The bridge was destroyed by the storm."; "Volunteers cleaned the beach." becomes "The beach was cleaned by volunteers."
grammar.commonMistake: Mixing up was and were with plural subjects: "The trees was planted" must be "The trees were planted", because a plural subject always takes were.
grammar.memoryTip: Match the helper to the subject before adding the participle: singular subject, was plus past participle; plural subject, were plus past participle.
grammar.practice:
Part A — rewrite each active sentence in the past passive: 1) A local farmer discovered the rare bird. 2) Heavy rains flooded the village last year. 3) The government built a new wildlife sanctuary. 4) Illegal loggers destroyed hundreds of trees. 5) Students organised an environmental awareness day.
Part B — two more to rewrite: 6) Volunteers planted two hundred trees last month. 7) The students documented the damage.

Answer Key (for self-checking):
Part A: 1) The rare bird was discovered by a local farmer. 2) The village was flooded by heavy rains last year. 3) A new wildlife sanctuary was built by the government. 4) Hundreds of trees were destroyed by illegal loggers. 5) An environmental awareness day was organised by students.
Part B: 6) Two hundred trees were planted by volunteers last month. 7) The damage was documented by the students.

grammar.title: Modal Verbs + Passive
grammar.explanation: Combining a modal verb such as must, should, can, may, might or could with the passive lets you state rules, advice, possibilities and permissions without naming who acts. This pattern is very common in environmental discussions and formal writing.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: subject + modal verb + be + past participle.
Obligation: "Endangered species must be protected by law." Advice: "More trees should be planted in urban areas." Possibility: "Renewable energy can be used to power entire cities." Permission: "The park may be visited between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m." Negative: "Plastic bags must not be thrown into the ocean."
grammar.commonMistake: Leaving out "be" or adding an extra "is": "Pollution must stopped" and "The forest is must be protected" are both wrong — the pattern is always modal, then be, then the past participle.
grammar.memoryTip: Chant the three-word chain modal-be-done: must be protected, should be reduced, can be achieved. The middle word be never changes, whatever the modal.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence using the modal in brackets and the passive voice: 1) Water pollution ______ (must / reduce) immediately. 2) More national parks ______ (should / establish) to protect wildlife. 3) Plastic waste ______ (can / recycle) into useful products. 4) Forests ______ (must / not / destroy) for short-term profit. 5) Environmental awareness ______ (should / teach) in every school. 6) Clean energy solutions ______ (can / develop) with enough research.
Part B — rewrite in the passive: 7) People must not dump waste in rivers. 8) The government should establish more national parks.

Answer Key (for self-checking):
Part A: 1) must be reduced 2) should be established 3) can be recycled 4) must not be destroyed 5) should be taught 6) can be developed.
Part B: 7) Waste must not be dumped in rivers (by people). 8) More national parks should be established (by the government).

grammar.title: Expressing the Future
grammar.explanation: English uses three main forms for the future, and each signals something different: will for predictions, promises and sudden decisions; going to for settled plans and evidence-based predictions; and the present continuous for fixed arrangements.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Will (subject + will + base verb) — prediction: "I think it will rain this afternoon." Promise: "I will help you carry the camping equipment." Spontaneous decision: "It's getting cold. I will put on my jacket." Negative: "Don't worry, it won't take long to reach the summit."
Going to (subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb) — plan: "We are going to visit the Boni Forest next Saturday." Intention: "I am going to write a report on deforestation." Evidence: "Look at the sky — it is going to rain soon."
Present continuous (subject + am/is/are + verb-ing with a future time word) — "We are leaving at 6 a.m. tomorrow." "The conservation team is meeting on Friday morning." "I am volunteering at the tree-planting event this weekend."
To choose: prediction or sudden decision, use will; decided plan or visible evidence, use going to; arrangement with a set time or place, use the present continuous.
grammar.commonMistake: Using "will" for a plan that is already decided: if the visit is settled, "I will visit the park tomorrow" should be "I am going to visit the park tomorrow"; watch also for dropping am, is or are, as in "She going to help".
grammar.memoryTip: Ask which situation you are in before choosing: sudden or predicted → will; decided or evidence in front of you → going to; booked with a time and place → present continuous.
grammar.practice:
Part A — choose the best future form for each sentence: 1) The eco-club ______ (meet) at the school gate at 7 a.m. on Saturday. (fixed arrangement) 2) I think solar energy ______ (replace) fossil fuels one day. (general prediction) 3) We have decided — we ______ (organise) a beach clean-up next month. (plan already decided) 4) That tree looks unstable. It ______ (fall) in the next storm. (evidence-based prediction) 5) The rain has stopped! I ______ (go) outside for a walk. (spontaneous decision) 6) They ______ (fly) to Nairobi on Tuesday for the conference. (fixed arrangement)
Part B — three more from your lesson booklet: 7) Look at the weather forecast — it ______ (snow) tonight. (evidence-based prediction) 8) We ______ (camp) by the lake this weekend; everything is booked. (fixed arrangement) 9) Wait — I ______ (help) you set up the tent. (spontaneous offer)

Answer Key (for self-checking):
Part A: 1) is meeting — fixed arrangement. 2) will replace — general prediction. 3) are going to organise — plan already decided. 4) is going to fall — evidence-based prediction. 5) will go — spontaneous decision. 6) are flying — fixed arrangement.
Part B: 7) is going to snow — evidence-based prediction. 8) are camping — fixed arrangement, already booked. 9) will help — spontaneous offer.

grammar.title: Comparative and Superlative Forms
grammar.explanation: Comparative and superlative adjectives let you weigh choices — which energy source is cleaner, which forest is the largest, which approach is the most effective — so they power persuasive environmental writing and debate.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Comparatives (two things): one-syllable adjectives add -er (tall → taller, clean → cleaner); one syllable ending in -e adds -r (large → larger, safe → safer); one-syllable consonant-vowel-consonant doubles the final consonant (hot → hotter, big → bigger); two syllables ending in -y change -y to -i and add -er (happy → happier, easy → easier); longer adjectives use more (beautiful → more beautiful, sustainable → more sustainable).
Superlatives (three or more things): add -est (tall → tallest), change -y to -iest (happy → happiest), or use most (beautiful → most beautiful).
Irregular forms: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst; far → farther or further → farthest or furthest; little → less → least; much and many → more → most.
Examples: "Solar energy is cleaner than coal." "This is the tallest tree in the forest." "Hiking is more enjoyable than sitting indoors." "That was the most exciting expedition we have ever been on." "This solution is better than the one we tried before."
grammar.commonMistake: Doubling the comparison or using "more" with a short adjective: "more easier" and "more tall" are wrong — choose one form only, easier and taller.
grammar.memoryTip: Count the syllables: one syllable takes -er or -est, adjectives ending in -y swap to -ier or -iest, and longer adjectives put more or most in front instead.
grammar.practice:
Part A — write the correct comparative or superlative form: 1) The Amazon is the ______ (large) rainforest in the world. 2) Wind power is ______ (efficient) than many people think. 3) This path is ______ (steep) than the other one. 4) Recycling is one of the ______ (easy) ways to help the environment. 5) Deforestation is ______ (bad) now than it was ten years ago. 6) This national park is the ______ (beautiful) place I have ever visited. 7) Walking is ______ (healthy) than driving. 8) This is the ______ (good) camping trip we have ever had.
Part B — five more from your lesson booklet: 9) The Boni Forest is one of the ______ (rare) forests in East Africa. 10) Solar energy is ______ (clean) than burning coal. 11) Planting trees is one of the ______ (effective) ways to fight climate change. 12) This campsite is ______ (comfortable) than the last one because it has shade. 13) Protecting biodiversity is ______ (important) than many people realise.

Answer Key (for self-checking):
Part A: 1) largest 2) more efficient 3) steeper 4) easiest 5) worse 6) most beautiful 7) healthier 8) best.
Part B: 9) rarest 10) cleaner 11) most effective 12) more comfortable 13) more important.

writing.title: Writing 1: Trip Guide for Younger Students
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a trip guide for younger students at your school who are about to go on their first outdoor expedition. Include a short introduction saying where the trip goes and why it is exciting; a section on what to pack (equipment, clothing, food and water); a section on safety tips such as staying on the marked trail and what to do if you get lost; a section on respecting the environment, including leave no trace and collecting litter; and an encouraging conclusion. Use imperatives for instructions ("Pack a waterproof jacket."), future forms for what will happen ("You will hike through beautiful scenery."), -ing forms ("Exploring nature is the best way to learn about the environment.") and comparatives for advice ("Boots are more comfortable than sandals for hiking."). Write at least 250 words and check your spelling, grammar and punctuation before submitting.
writing.modelText: A strong trip guide speaks directly to its younger readers, orders its sections clearly, gives instructions as imperatives, and uses future forms and comparatives to make the advice practical.
writing.successCriteria: I addressed the prompt and audience; organised ideas into cohesive paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported claims with relevant evidence; considered viewpoint and source reliability; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Plan claims, topic sentences and supporting evidence, then use the word bank and source models.
writing.extension: Synthesize details from more than one text, acknowledge an alternative viewpoint, vary sentence structures and strengthen the conclusion.

writing.title: Writing 2: Environmental Protection Speech
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a speech for a school assembly about why students should care about the environment and what actions they can take. Open with something that grabs attention: a question, a surprising fact or a very short story. Highlight two or three environmental problems such as deforestation, pollution or loss of biodiversity, then give practical actions students can take, and close with words that inspire the audience to act. Use the passive to describe problems ("Forests are being destroyed at an alarming rate."), modal verbs for obligation and possibility ("We must act now.", "Change can be achieved."), -ing forms ("Reducing our waste is something every student can do."), future forms for your vision, and rhetorical questions to involve your listeners. Write at least 300 words and practise reading the speech aloud before your final draft.
writing.modelText: A strong speech hooks the audience in its first line, names real problems in the passive, presents actions with modals such as must and can, and ends with a vision the listeners want to join.

writing.title: Writing 3: Jamal's Diary Entry

quizzes.quizTitle: Outdoor Adventures and Environmental Protection checkpoint
quizzes.question: What does 'acknowledge' mean?
quizzes.options: A serious effort or attempt to do something. | To accept or admit that something is true, or to recognise that you have received something. | To create or start something that is meant to last. | To show how something works or to prove something clearly.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: To accept or admit that something is true, or to recognise that you have received something. Example: I want to acknowledge that you did a great job on your project.
To make something less severe, harmful or serious. Example: Building a dam will mitigate the damage caused by future floods.
To give up or let go of something, especially power or a right. Example: She decided to relinquish her position as club president at the end of the year.
To damage or spoil something, especially a reputation or quality. Example: Illegal dumping can tarnish the beauty of a national park.
embellish — Jamal 'did not try to embellish the facts' in his report; none of the other options fits the idea of adding untrue detail.
collaboration — the ranger's exact words are 'Protecting the forest is not one person's job — it requires collaboration.'
was polluted — the past passive, formed with was plus the past participle, because 'last year' signals a finished past event.
be protected — the modal must is always followed by be and the past participle in the passive.
learning — after the preposition 'in', the verb must take the -ing form.
are visiting — a fixed arrangement with a set day takes the present continuous.
